Issued at 208 PM EDT Wed Oct 14 2026

Rest of Today-Tonight...Drier air lingers across the area today,
with PWATs near 1". That, combined with subsidence aloft from high
pressure across the Deep South has limited most shower development
today. However, a few very isolated light showers embedded within
the stratocu field have been noted on KMLB radar today. Thus, have
maintained a low, 15-20%, PoP area-wide today. CAMs still suggest
a few showers are possible this afternoon west of Orlando prior to
sunset. Regardless, mostly dry conditions persist, though showers
will be possible along the coast overnight. They may occasionally
drift onshore, embedded within easterly flow. Warm highs in the
mid to upper 80s will remain in the lower to mid-70s tonight.
Coastal areas look to linger in the upper 70s with winds 5-10 mph
from the east.

Thursday-Friday...The ridge moves off of the Southeast coast 
tomorrow, then farther into the Atlantic Friday, as a trough digs 
through the northern US. This trough will then push a surface 
front into the central Florida peninsula Friday night. Onshore
flow prevails through the period, increasing to 10-15 mph once
again Thursday afternoon. However, winds remain overall light
Friday, reaching only 10 mph along the coast behind the diffuse sea
breeze. Moisture builds northward through the period, with
scattered showers and storms (30-50%) forecast south of Melbourne
in the afternoon. From around Orlando northward, drier conditions
are forecast, though a low chance (20%) for coastal showers will
linger overnight. PWATs near 2" will support increased coverage
(60%) of showers and storms area-wide Friday, with a possible sea
breeze collision over the far interior late. Overall, the threat
for strong storms is low, with warm temperatures aloft -5 to -6 C,
but a gust or two to 45 mph cannot be ruled out. Temperatures 
climb to slightly above normal, in the upper 80s to near 90 late 
week, as overnight lows remain in the 70s.

Saturday-Tuesday...The surface front is forecast to reach south 
Florida Saturday morning. However, the mid-level trough looks to 
lag behind slightly, passing through central Florida through day. 
The front then looks to remain stalled in the vicinity of south 
Florida into early next week, as strong ridging builds over the 
eastern US, north of the Florida peninsula. A tight pressure 
gradient between the front and the ridge will lead to windy 
conditions rapidly developing from north to south Saturday, which 
linger through the weekend and into early next week. Daybreak to 
begin the weekend may even have generally light northerly flow. 
However, by Saturday afternoon, sustained NNE winds build to 15-25
mph and gusts to 25-35 mph. Winds only further increase into 
Sunday and Monday as they veer ENE, with winds 20-25 mph area-wide
and gusts 30-40 mph. The highest winds are forecast along the 
coast, remaining breezy to windy overnight. Breezy conditions 
inland will become windy into the afternoon, with daytime heating.
Needless to say, Wind Advisories are likely through the weekend 
and into early next week, with conditions persisting through the 
forecast period.

With the front stalled across southern Florida, PWATs look to remain 
up to 1.6-2" south of Cape Canaveral. This, combined with stout 
onshore flow, will lead to multiple rounds of fast-moving showers 
moving into coastal areas. Portions of the southern coast are 
highlighted in a Marginal Risk for excessive rainfall (1/4) this 
weekend. The greatest threat looks to be along the Treasure Coast, 
where training bands of showers are likely. 90th percentile 48 hour 
rainfall accumulations of 3-5" are forecast for the Marginal Risk 
area Saturday into Sunday. However, portions of Martin and St Lucie 
Counties have a 25% chance of exceeding 4" during the same period. 
Thus, will need to monitor the threat for flooding, especially in 
areas that have seen recent heavy rainfall. PoPs 60-80% are forecast 
for the southern coast through early next week. Elsewhere, drier air 
filtering into the area will limit the heavy rainfall threat, with 
PoPs 20-50%. The threat for strong storms will be low due to warm 
temperatures aloft (-6 C at 500mb). Though showers or storms may 
locally enhance the already windy flow.

High temperatures fall into the upper 70s to lower 80s through
early next week, as lows fall into the upper 60s to lower 70s. This
prolonged period of strong onshore flow will lead to dangerous 
beach and boating conditions. Gale- force wind gusts look to 
produce high surf, with breaking waves 9-12 ft. Multiple tidal 
cycles of high surf will also contribute to up to moderate beach 
erosion, especially north of Cape Canaveral. Residents and 
visitors should use caution near the beach and remain out of the 
water.
